extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and policymakers considering the proposed U.S. Constitution (readers of The Federalist Papers)
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and practical safeguards concerning the size and augmentation of the House of Representatives and the allocation of power to regulate federal elections (times, places, and manner). Focused on constitutional design trade-offs between state and national authority, majority rule, and effective representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision for periodic augmentation of representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The number which is to prevail in the first instance is declared to be temporary. Its duration is limited to the short term of three years. Within every successive term of ten years a census of inhabitants is to be repeated. The unequivocal objects of these regulations are, first, to readjust, from time to time, the apportionment of representatives to the number of inhabitants, under the single exception that each State shall have one representative at least; secondly, to augment the number of representatives at the same periods, under the sole limitation that the whole number shall not exceed one for every thirty thousand inhabitants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This constitutional mechanism (temporary initial size, decennial census, reapportionment, upper population limit of one per 30,000) is presented as a deliberate safeguard to ensure representation keeps pace with population growth and is superior to mere directory provisions in some state constitutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larger states will advocate increasing representatives (bicameral check)
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of the legislature is a representation of citizens, the other of the States: in the former, consequently, the larger States will have most weight; in the latter, the advantage will be in favor of the smaller States. From this circumstance it may with certainty be inferred that the larger States will be strenuous advocates for increasing the number and weight of that part of the legislature in which their influence predominates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the bicameral structure (House representing people, Senate representing states), political incentives will push larger states to press for augmentation when population warrants it; coalition dynamics (a few large states can form majority) and the interests of growing new states further promote reapportionment.

rubrics_metrics.name: House control of the purse as an instrument to secure augmentation and redress
rubrics_metrics.description: The House of Representatives cannot only refuse, but they alone can propose, the supplies requisite for the support of government. They, in a word, hold the purse that powerful instrument by which ... an infant and humble representation of the people gradually enlarging the sphere of its activity and importance ... This power over the purse may, in fact, be regarded as the most complete and effectual weapon with which any constitution can arm the immediate representatives of the people, for obtaining a redress of every grievance, and for carrying into effect every just and salutary measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The budgetary/initiation-of-supplies power gives the House leverage to obtain constitutional augmentations and protections of its authority; historical analogy to British practice is used to justify this as a practical check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule and dangers of raising quorum/decision thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been said that more than a majority ought to have been required for a quorum; and in particular cases, if not in all, more than a majority of a quorum for a decision. But these considerations are outweighed by the inconveniences in the opposite scale. In all cases where justice or the general good might require new laws to be passed, or active measures to be pursued, the fundamental principle of free government would be reversed. It would be no longer the majority that would rule: the power would be transferred to the minority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requiring supermajorities for quorum or decision would empower minorities to obstruct needed measures, enable interested minorities to shield themselves from equitable sacrifices, facilitate secessions, and subvert order; thus simple majority rule is defended as essential to free government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimal assembly size: secure sufficient number then avoid excess
rubrics_metrics.description: After securing a sufficient number for the purposes of safety, of local information, and of diffusive sympathy with the whole society, they will counteract their own views by every addition to their representatives. The countenance of the government may become more democratic, but the soul that animates it will be more oligarchic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Larger assemblies increase the proportion of members of limited information and weak capacities, magnify the ascendancy of passion and eloquence of the few, and thereby may make the assembly easier to be directed by a small, artful minority. Thus there is a normative tradeoff: enough representatives to ensure safety/local knowledge, but not so many that effective deliberation and quality of decision decline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every government ought to contain in itself the means of its own preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: The propriety rests upon this plain proposition, that every government ought to contain in itself the means of its own preservation. ... It will therefore not be denied, that a discretionary power over elections ought to exist somewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is offered as a foundational standard for allocating the ultimate authority to regulate elections: because no single fixed election law could suit all future circumstances, some entity must retain power to act to preserve the government (here, the national legislature as a last resort).

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of leaving exclusive control of federal elections to State legislatures
rubrics_metrics.description: An exclusive power of regulating elections for the national government, in the hands of the State legislatures, would leave the existence of the Union entirely at their mercy. They could at any moment annihilate it, by neglecting to provide for the choice of persons to administer its affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if such neglect is improbable in practice, the constitutional possibility is intolerable; therefore preserving a national right to regulate 'times, places, and manner' is necessary to prevent dissolution of the Union through state inaction or conspiracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural differences between Senate and House mitigate risks differently
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be easily discerned also that the national government would run a much greater risk from a power in the State legislatures over the elections of its House of Representatives, than from their power of appointing the members of its Senate. The senators are to be chosen for the period of six years; there is to be a rotation ... and no State is to be entitled to more than two senators; a quorum of the body is to consist of sixteen members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of longer terms, rotation, small per-state allotment, and quorum rules, the Senate is less vulnerable to temporary combinations of state legislatures seeking to impair the Union; the House, with biennial elections, is much more sensitive to state control of election regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State legislators' local interests may conflict with national welfare
rubrics_metrics.description: The people of America may be warmly attached to the government of the Union, at times when the particular rulers of particular States, stimulated by the natural rivalship of power, and by the hopes of personal aggrandizement, and supported by a strong faction in each of those States, may be in a very opposite temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State rulers, motivated by ambition or faction, might conspire to prevent federal elections or otherwise subvert the Union; this realpolitik concern supports reserving ultimate national authority over times/places/manner of elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbability that national regulation of times/places/manner would be used to favor a class
rubrics_metrics.description: It is alleged that [national regulation] might be employed in such a manner as to promote the election of some favorite class of men in exclusion of others, by confining the places of election to particular districts ... Of all chimerical suppositions, this seems to be the most chimerical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hamilton rejects this fear: such measures would provoke popular revolt and state resistance; additionally, diversity of interests, differing branch constituencies, and the inclusion of the Senate make coordinated national manipulation unlikely in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: No practical way to elevate 'the wealthy and the well-born' via time/place regulations alone
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no method of securing to the rich the preference apprehended, but by prescribing qualifications of property either for those who may elect or be elected. But this forms no part of the power to be conferred upon the national government. Its authority would be expressly restricted to the regulation of the TIMES, the PLACES, the MANNER of elections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the national power is limited to procedural regulation (time/place/manner) and not to qualifications, procedural regulation alone cannot lawfully or practically be used to impose property tests or formally exclude classes from participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: National government less likely than states to favor narrow economic interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Because national representation is an emanation from a greater variety of interests, and in much more various proportions, than are to be found in any single State, it will be much less apt to espouse either [landed or mercantile] with a decided partiality, than the representation of any single State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to fears of bias toward landed or mercantile interests: aggregate national representation dilutes narrow local majorities and thereby reduces the risk of the Union's councils favoring a particular economic class to the detriment of others.
